Back in the 1920s, Romania was a tough place, with poverty and disease everywhere. That's where our story kicks off. Willem Zeffer, an American talent agent, and his Romanian-born actress client, Katya Lupi, had traveled there to visit Katya's relatives. Willem stumbled upon an old medieval castle that had been turned into a monastery. There, he bought a unique piece of art—a series of sculpted and painted tiles depicting a local legend. The legend told of a Count cursed to haunt the nearby wilderness forever, and the tiles showed it in a grotesque, obscene way.

Fast forward to the year 2000. Todd Pickett, a fading movie star, decided to undergo plastic surgery to look younger and make a comeback. But something went wrong, leaving Todd disfigured. He had to hide out during his recovery. His agent chose Katya Lupi's old home, an abandoned house in Coldheart Canyon, a secluded spot outside Hollywood. But Todd soon found out that Katya and her "subjects" were still around, holding court.

text: A 10-year-old boy named Measle is living with his horrid guardian, Basil Tramplebone. Measle's life is horrible and boring. Basil builds a detailed train set out using money that was left for Measle by his parents and plays with it, while all Measle can do is watch him. Desperate to play with it, Measle tricks Basil into leaving the house by telling him that there is extra money in the bank. His plan backfires, and Basil catches him playing with the train set when he gets home. Basil magically shrinks Measle and placed him in the train set. In a grim, windowless brick house live the Twits, a couple so nasty they make a art out of making each other miserable. Mr. and Mrs. Twit are locked in a never-ending prank war, fueled by pure spite. Meanwhile, the Twits' pet monkeys, the Muggle-Wumps, were forced to stand on their heads, the Twits dreaming of a monkey circus. But the monkeys had had enough.

With the help of the Roly-Poly Bird, a clever creature from other tales, they hatched a plan. While the Twits were out, they used Mr. Twit's super glue to stick all their furniture to the ceiling. When the Twits returned, they were tricked into thinking they were upside down. The glue held them fast, and they started to shrink—just like Mr. Twit had fooled Mrs. Twit earlier. They shrank right out of existence, leaving the Muggle-Wumps free at last. The Roly-Poly Bird made sure other birds knew to avoid the sticky trees, and the monkeys finally got their happy ending.

text: Lolla-Wossiky, a troubled, one-eyed, whiskey "Red", leaves General Harrison's fort and heads north in order to find his "dream beast", the spirit that can save him from the pain of his memories. On his journey, he meets Alvin Miller and assists him in making an ethical decision that will shape his life forever. In appreciation, Alvin heals Lolla-Wossiky painful memories, allowing him to give up alcohol and become in touch with the land once again. Lolla-Wossiky grows into "the Prophet" although he prefers to be known as Tenskwa-Tawa. Lolla-Wossiky preaches both pacifism and separatism, believing that "Reds" should live west of the Mississippi and "Whites" should live east of it. Meanwhile, Lolla-Wossiky's brother, Ta-Kumsaw, tries to rally "Reds" behind his belief that their land should be defended violently. When Alvin Miller and his older brother Measure travel to the place of his birth (where Alvin is expected to become apprenticed to the Hatrack River blacksmith) the two brothers are captured by 'Reds' (Native Americans) sent by William Henry Harrison to intentionally create conflict. Ta-Kumsaw, sent by Lolla-Wossiky, rescues the brothers from torture and death. Measure leaves the "Reds" only to be captured by William Henry Harrison's men and subsequently beaten to the brink of death. Ta-Kumsaw accompanies Alvin to the holy site of Eight-Face Mound where they meet up with Taleswapper, an old friend of Alvin. Using the spiritual powers of the Eight-Face Mound, Alvin is able to heal Measure from afar. Measure is then able to stop some of the slaughter of Lolla-Wossiky's followers by villagers and William Henry Harrison's men over the alleged kidnapping and murder of Alvin and Measure Miller.

text:
A broken, one-eyed man known as Lolla-Wossiky—nicknamed the Red for his love of whiskey—leaves the fortified settlement of General Harrison to seek out a mythic spirit, the “dream beast,” believing it could heal his haunted memories. His quest takes a transformative turn when he encounters Alvin Miller, a man facing his own moral crossroads. Guided by Lolla-Wossiky’s presence, Alvin makes a choice that will deeply affect his life. In gratitude, Lolla-Wossiky’s suffering is lifted as his painful memories are mended, allowing him to renounce alcohol and reconnect with the natural world. Over time, Lolla-Wossiky emerges as “the Prophet,” though he prefers the name Tenskwa-Tawa. Alongside his brother Ta-Kumsaw, who advocates for violent resistance among their people, Lolla-Wossiky develops a dual message: teaching both pacifism and the need for a separate, geographically defined existence—“Reds” to the west of the Mississippi, “Whites” to the east.

Meanwhile, trouble brews when Alvin and his brother Measure are captured by Native Americans—referred to in the records as “Reds”—who are incited by President William Henry Harrison to provoke conflict. Ta-Kumsaw, going in search of his brother, manages to rescue Measure from certain death. Measure, however, is later recaptured by Harrison’s forces and left for the brink of death. At the sacred Eight-Face Mound, with the help of an old friend, Taleswapper, Alvin channels powerful spiritual forces to heal Measure from a distance. This intervention proves decisive when Measure is able to stop the massacre of Lolla-Wossiky’s followers by local villagers and Harrison’s troops, who had accused the group of kidnapping and murdering the Miller brothers. Through these events, Lolla-Wossiky’s vision of separation and peace, as well as his personal redemption, take on new meaning in the face of violence and division.

Lolla-Wossiky, a troubled and one-eyed drifter known as the “Red,” leaves General Harrison’s fort and sets north in search of his “dream beast”—a spirit he hopes can help him escape the agony of his memories. On his journey, he encounters Alvin Miller and helps him make a crucial ethical choice that will profoundly affect Alvin’s life. Grateful, Alvin uses his powers to heal Lolla-Wossiky’s painful memories. Through this healing, Lolla-Wossiky abandons alcohol and reconnects with the land. Over time, he becomes known as the Prophet, though he prefers the name Tenskwa-Tawa.

While Lolla-Wossiky preaches both pacifism and the idea of separatism—the belief that “Reds” should live west of the Mississippi and “Whites” east of it—his brother Ta-Kumsaw takes a different path. He tries to organize “Reds” to defend their land through violence.

When the Miller brothers return to their birthplace, hoping Alvin will apprentice with the Hatrack River blacksmith, they are captured by Native Americans identified as “Reds,” sent by President William Henry Harrison to stoke conflict. Ta-Kumsaw, sent by Lolla-Wossiky, rescues Alvin and Measure from certain death and torture. However, Measure is soon recaptured by Harrison’s men and left for death, barely surviving. Ta-Kumsaw accompanies Alvin to the sacred site of Eight-Face Mound. There, with the help of Taleswapper, an old friend of Alvin’s, Alvin channels the mound’s spiritual power to heal Measure remotely. With Measure restored, he is able to intervene and halt part of the massacre of Lolla-Wossiky’s followers by local villagers and Harrison’s troops, who blame the incident on the alleged kidnapping and murder of the Millers.

text: The story centers on G. Gordon Gregg, a surgeon whose meticulous brutality mirrors that of H. H. Holmes. He targets young, beautiful women, drawing them into his elaborate, maze-like castle where he kills them with clinical precision and minimal suffering—each death engineered to avoid detection. text: The story is episodic. First we learn of Stuart's birth to a family in New York City and how the family adapts, socially and structurally, to having such a small son. He has an adventure in which he gets caught in a window-blind while exercising, and Snowbell, the family cat, places Stuart's hat and cane outside a mouse hole, panicking the family. He is accidentally released by his brother George. Then two chapters describe Stuart's participation in a boat race in Central Park. A bird named Margalo is adopted by the Little family, and Stuart protects her from their malevolent cat. The bird repays his kindness by saving Stuart when he is trapped in a garbage can and shipped out for disposal at sea. Margalo flees when she is warned that one of Snowbell's friends intends to eat her, and Stuart strikes out to find her and bring her home. A friendly dentist, who is also the owner of the boat Stuart had raced in Central Park, gives him use of a gasoline-powered model car, and Stuart departs to see the country. He works for a while as a substitute teacher and comes to the town of Ames Crossing, where he meets a girl named Harriet Ames who is no taller than he is. They go on one date, and then Stuart leaves town. As the book ends, he has not yet found Margalo, but feels confident he will do so.

text:
Stuart Little, born to a family in New York City, shakes up their world. His tiny size forces them to adapt, socially and structurally. One day, Stuart gets stuck in a window-blind while exercising, causing a panic. The family cat, Snowbell, adds to the chaos by placing Stuart's hat and cane outside a mouse hole. Later, Stuart accidentally escapes with his brother George's help.

Next, Stuart joins a boat race in Central Park. The Little family adopts a bird named Margalo, and Stuart protects her from their malevolent cat. In return, Margalo saves Stuart when he's trapped in a garbage can, destined for disposal at sea. She flees after learning Snowbell's friend wants to eat her. Stuart sets out to find her.

A friendly dentist, who owns the boat Stuart raced in Central Park, lends him a gasoline-powered model car. Stuart hits the road, seeing the country. He even works as a substitute teacher for a while. In Ames Crossing, he meets Harriet Ames, a girl his size. They go on a date, but Stuart soon leaves town.

The story ends with Stuart still searching for Margalo, but he's confident he'll find her.

text:
After their son Eddie’s tragic death from a hit-and-run, Henry’s family is forced to leave their old neighborhood, hoping to distance themselves from the pain that lingers in every corner. Eddie’s loss left his father withdrawn and silent, unable to work anymore, while his mother’s job at the local store becomes her only steady anchor. Henry helps the family by working at the grocery, where the owner, Mr. Hairston, is both demanding and sharp-tongued, often making offensive remarks to the customers who pass through his shop. He always seems extra attentive to Henry, which makes the atmosphere there feel both tense and uneasy.

Another difficulty Henry faces is that there’s no proper grave marker for Eddie. The lack of a resting place weighs heavy on the family, and Henry’s sense of duty to honor Eddie pushes him to find a solution. One day, while lingering at the store, Henry mentions the odd, reclusive old man who is always leaving the nearby "crazy house" and heading down the street. To his surprise, the man is Mr. Levine, a Holocaust survivor whose face holds stories and sorrow beneath his gentle eyes. Henry becomes acquainted with Mr. Levine at the art center, where Levine carves and arranges miniature models of his lost hometown.

One evening, Henry confides in Mr. Hairston about his encounters with Mr. Levine. Mr. Hairston’s reaction is immediate and unexpected—he offers to buy a gravestone for Eddie if Henry follows his instructions. But his motives soon grow ambiguous. Before long, Mr. Hairston tells Henry that he’ll be let go from the store if he doesn’t comply with another demand: he must destroy Mr. Levine’s carefully built model village at the art center. If Henry does this, Mr. Hairston promises better things for his mother—a raise and security for his job—and promises to keep Henry’s good behavior intact. However, Mr. Hairston makes it clear that he has connections with Henry’s principal and his mother’s employer and that failure to cooperate could ruin Henry’s chances at school and his mother’s career.

Torn between loyalty to his family and the weight of Mr. Hairston’s threat, Henry spends the night at the art center, wrestling with what to do. He nearly destroys the model village with a mallet when a startled rat makes him flinch and he drops the mallet instead, damaging the village in the process. On his way home, Mr. Hairston confronts him on the street and reveals his true motive: he wanted Henry to destroy the village because Levine is Jewish, and Mr. Hairston resented him. He saw this act as a way to torment Henry and punish him for being too kind to someone perceived as different.

In the end, Henry refuses the reward. His family soon returns to their old town, perhaps seeking a quieter peace and a fresh start away from the shadows cast by those who would manipulate their pain.

text:
Henry’s family moves to a new town, hoping to escape the heavy shadows left by their son Eddie, who died after being hit by a car whose driver vanished without a trace. Eddie’s death left Henry’s father withdrawn and silent, no longer able to work, while his mother works long hours just to keep the family going. The added burden for Henry is that there is no proper grave marker for Eddie—no stone to rest him beneath.

At the local grocery, Henry works for Mr. Hairston, a sharp-tongued old man who makes crude remarks to the customers who pass his store. Yet, Mr. Hairston seems especially interested in Henry, perhaps even too so. Working under such an exacting man, Henry learns patience—though Mr. Hairston’s criticism is always just a step away from belittling his own family as well.

Every day, Henry notices an elderly man slipping away from the house now labeled the ‘crazy house,’ where Eddie died. Curious, Henry follows the figure one afternoon and discovers he is Mr. Levine, an old man who introduces himself at the nearby art center. Mr. Levine is a Holocaust survivor, haunted by the loss of his family to the SS. Each day, he carves meticulous models of his old hometown—a silent act of remembrance.

One evening, Henry confides in Mr. Hairston about Mr. Levine. To his surprise, the grocer agrees to help find a suitable gravestone for Eddie. But days later, Mr. Hairston delivers bad news: he’ll be let go from the store at the week’s end unless Henry destroys Mr. Levine’s model village. He adds that his connections reach as far as his mother’s boss and Henry’s principal, threatening to ruin both jobs if Henry refuses. The only reward if Henry destroys the village: his mother's raise, his job saved, and the grave sculpture as a keepsake.

Torn between loyalty and fear, Henry waits at the art center through the night, considering what to do. Just as he lifts the mallet to destroy the village, a startled rat causes him to drop the tool, damaging part of the miniature landscape. The next day on the street, Mr. Hairston explains his true motive: “Because he’s a Jew,” he says, hoping to torment Henry by robbing him of the supposed “reward” and his sense of being ‘a good boy.’ Henry refuses both the reward and Mr. Hairston’s pressure. Eventually, after this confrontation, Henry’s family returns to their original town.

text:
Shadows lengthen across the office at Angel Investigations that particular afternoon, the air oddly tense despite the usual hum of paperwork and the banter between team members. A frantic figure bursts in, breathless, pursued by a grotesque, snarling demon. The team springs into action; soon, dust settles on the creature’s charred, dissolution as it collapses, its form already crumbling away. But the real shock comes from the man’s story—he claims he’s been targeted by a demon pretending to be Angel, and now he’s mistrustful of the whole operation, clutching a strange, ancient stone found in what he believes was someone else’s name.

Angel is unsettled by the thought of a demonic impostor, especially one so close. Cordy, more skeptical than usual, just smirks and wonders aloud why the fake Angel would go for less than Hollywood’s finest. Meanwhile, Lorne reports an unmistakable surge of dark energy emanating from Caritas, enough to rattle even his usual composure. Something’s disturbing the city’s demon population, making even the most placid beings bristly and unpredictable.

Investigation reveals the culprit: David, a photography student with a taste for drama, witnessed Angel’s deeds in early L.A. and, for reasons unclear, has taken to impersonating him. His motive isn’t greed or revenge—it’s the rush of power that comes with besting demons. Cordelia and Fred dig deeper and uncover the stone’s true origin: it’s a burial marker from another realm. Used to commemorate demons who perished in battle, the stones capture the feelings of death—specifically, the rage of a warrior who recently died in a fierce conflict. Normally, spells would contain these energies, but absent those rituals, the stone’s emotions are leaking out, infecting nearby demons and heightening their aggression.

As chaos erupts outside the office, the team realizes the stone’s owner is desperate to recover it for their lost kin. A swarm of demonic adversaries closes in, their moods heightened by the stone’s influence. In the ensuing fight, Angel finds himself gripped by a nearly overwhelming fury, on the verge of losing control. That changes when David steps forward, risking himself to save Angel. His selfless sacrifice gives Angel the space he needs—a moment to calm his anger and focus.

In that instant, Angel destroys the stone, shattering the wave of hostile emotion and bringing the demon horde under control. Though the day ends in loss for David, it is a small victory for truth and self-control, reminding Angel—and everyone else—how fragile the line is between power and restraint.

Normally, rituals in the demons’ world would kept these emotions contained, but without them, the stone’s feelings are leaking out, infecting nearby demons.

 It seems a quiet day at Angel Investigations until a desperate man arrives, chased by a demon. The gang kills the monster, which decomposes as soon as it dies. The man seems to have fallen victim to a stolen identity scam; he's been approached by a false Angel and is now distrustful of the real thing, so does not want to give up the ancient stone he's found. Angel's worried by the notion of an impersonator, but Cordy's just curious why he didn't impersonate more worthy celebrities. Meanwhile Lorne reports some bad mojo from Caritas, and needs help. Something is getting under local demons' skins, and even bothering Angel, heightening the aggression of normally rather pacifistic demons. As their research continues, Cordelia and Fred learn that the Angel-impersonator- a photography student called David who saw Angel in action during his early days in Los Angeles- is impersonating Angel for no reason other than the power trip he gets when defeating demons, and doesn't truly understand the reasons why Angel does what he does. The stone that David's client possesses is later revealed to be the burial stone of a race of demons whose nature causes them to disintegrate upon death caused them to start using the stones as a memorial, the stones 'recording' their feelings at the moment of death. The stone the client possesses contains the rage and hostility of an honoured warrior who recently died in battle; in their home dimension, the stone's 'emissions' would normally be controlled by various spells, but without those spells the emotions are spilling out and 'infecting' every demon in the area. In the final confrontation, as Angel and his associates attempt to aid the stone's owners in acquiring the stone while holding off a mass of demons, Angel nearly surrenders to his rage, but David's act of sacrifice during the battle, giving his life to save Angel's, gets through Angel's rage and allows him to focus long enough to allow the stone to be destroyed, thus ending the wave of hostility.

text: Each winter in Imardin, the capital city of Kyralia, the streets are purged of the "dwells", the city's poor under-class, by magicians who drive away the inhabitants of the city's slums. Although young gang members gather to throw rocks at them, the magicians are protected by a magical shield—until Sonea, a young dwell, hurls a rock through their barrier and injures the magician Lord Fergun. Fearing a rogue magician, the Guild begins searching for Sonea. Benign Lords Dannyl and Rothen lead the search into the slums, worried that Sonea's increasingly uncontrolled magic will harm her and those around her. But Sonea both distrusts the Guild for their apparent lack of compassion for the poor dwells and fears their reprisal for her accidental injury of Lord Fergun. She flees with her friend Cery, eventually seeking the aid of the shady Thieves, who see the value of having their own magician and take her under their care. With Cery, she sneaks into the Magician's Guild in an attempt to gain knowledge of how to control her magic, and observes a black-robed magician covered in blood performing a strange rite on a servant. However, her attempt is unsuccessful, and Sonea continues to lose control of her powers, setting fire to her surroundings repeatedly, before Lord Rothen at last locates her. Lord Rothen and the sinister Fergun fight for her mentorship, though Sonea herself is uninterested in training and only wants to return home to her friends and family. Lord Fergun attempts to sway Sonea to betray the Guild and thus "prove" that dwells are not fit to enter the Guild and goes so far as to kidnap and threaten Sonea's friend, Cery, but Fergun's plans are discovered and he will have to stand trial. In order to prove Fergun's guilt, Sonea submits to a mental examination, or 'truthreading' by Administrator Lorlen, who, finding the memory of the black-robed magician, reveal it to be Lord Akkarin, head of the guild, practising black magic – which is forbidden in Kyralia. Sonea decides then to join the Guild and train her magical potential.

text: During the winter in the capital city of Kyralia, magicians periodically clear the most impoverished districts, displacing the city’s poor, known as the "dwells." These evictions are typically carried out by magical forces, though they are usually protected by a shielding charm. This protection fails when a young girl named Sonea, a member of the dwells, manages to throw a stone and injure the powerful magician Lord Fergun. Worried that Sonea’s unpredictable magic could cause further harm, the Magician’s Guild launches a search for her, led by Lords Dannyl and Rothen. Sonea, however, feels little trust toward the Guild, seeing their actions as cold and indifferent to the dwells’ suffering. She also fears possible punishment from the Guild for harming Fergun. To avoid capture, Sonea flees with her companion Cery. Seeking guidance to manage her powers, she tries to infiltrate the Thieves’ community, hoping they might help her understand magic better. While there, Sonea watches a secretive ritual performed by a cloaked, blood-stained magician inside the Guild headquarters. Despite her efforts, she is unable to control her magic, and her powers cause destructive fires in the area. Eventually, Lord Rothen locates Sonea. Rothen and Fergun each try to persuade her to become a Guild apprentice and accept their mentorship, but Sonea is unwilling. Fergun, in a desperate move, kidnaps Cery to leverage Sonea’s cooperation. His plans are soon uncovered, and Fergun faces a formal trial. To provide evidence of Fergun’s wrongdoing, Sonea agrees to a mental examination conducted by Administrator Lorlen. The examination reveals that the blood-stained magician was actually the Guild’s own head, Lord Akkarin, who was secretly practicing forbidden black magic. Confronted with this truth, Sonea chooses to enter the Guild and begin training in order to master her abilities.

text:
In Imardin, Kyralia’s capital, the city’s poorest—called the “dwells”—are driven out each winter by magicians enforcing an order that maintains social distance. Though young gang members sometimes attack the magicians, these spellcasters are protected by magical shields, except when Sonea, a young resident of the slums, hurls a rock through the barrier and injures Lord Fergun. Concerned that Sonea’s uncontrollable magic could endanger herself and others, the Guild’s benefit-minded Lords Dannyl and Rothen launch a search for her.

Sonea resists their intervention, both distrustful of the Guild’s indifference to the dwells’ plight and fearful of reprisal for her accidental harm to Fergun. Fleeing with her friend Cery, she seeks out the Thieves’ Guild, who recognize the potential value of a powerful young mage and accept her. To gain control of her powers, Sonea enters the Magicians’ Guild under cover and watches a secretive ritual—an older, blood-stained magician performing a dark rite before a servant. Her efforts to understand magic go unfulfilled; Sonea’s powers continue to flare out of control, often setting fires around her.

Eventually, Lord Rothen locates Sonea. Rothen and the ambitious Lord Fergun both try to win her as a protégé, but Sonea refuses training, yearning only to return to her family in the slums. Fergun, desperate, kidnaps Cery to force Sonea’s compliance. However, Fergun’s schemes are exposed, and he is soon to face trial for his actions. To demonstrate Fergun’s wrongdoings, Sonea agrees to a mental examination by Administrator Lorlen. The truthreading reveals that the bloodied magician was actually Guild Head Akkarin, secretly dabbling in forbidden black magic. Moved by the evidence, Sonea decides to enter the Guild and begin training her abilities.

text: Under threat of execution after his conviction by the Time Lords at the end of The War Games, the Doctor is granted a reprieve if he agrees to undertake missions for the Celestial Intervention Agency. Accompanied and supervised by the ambitious Lady Serena, their first mission is to halt attacks upon three key figures in Earth's past: Napoleon Bonaparte, The Duke of Wellington, and Charles Maurice de Talleyrand. The Doctor re-encounters the Player known as the Countess and struggles to end her Grand Plan to allow Napoleon to win his various European campaigns. Her plan to set the City States of Europe against each other is stopped by the Doctor, despite her setting a Raston Warrior Robot and a vampire on him and Serena. In preventing the Countess's assassination scheme on Wellington, Serena is killed. The Countess has many back up plans, and at the Battle of Waterloo, her plan to prevent the Prussians coming to the English army's relief is thwarted when the Doctor imitates Napoleon himself to get through the French lines and deliver new orders to the Prussian commander. After returning to Gallifrey and discovering a traitor in the CIA who had been using the time scoop to assist the Countess, the Doctor is sent on a mission to investigate the time travel experiments of Kartz and Reimer.

text:
Gallifreyan authorities, threatened with execution after his court appearance in The War Games, forced the Doctor into a precarious bargain: he would serve the Celestial Intervention Agency in exchange for his freedom. Guided by the ambitious Lady Serena, his first assignment was to safeguard three pivotal historical figures—Napoleon Bonaparte, the Duke of Wellington, and Charles Maurice de Talleyrand—from violence across key moments in history. During these missions, the Doctor crossed paths with the enigmatic "Player," known as the Countess, whose convoluted Grand Plan sought to let Napoleon achieve military triumphs across Europe by turning the city-states against one another.

To carry out her schemes, the Countess deployed dangerous allies, including a Raston Warrior Robot and a vampire, against the Doctor and Serena. While attempting to stop her assassination plot targeting Wellington, Serena was fatally injured. The Countess proved remarkably resilient, devising multiple contingencies; one such plot culminated at the Battle of Waterloo, where she tried to prevent the Prussians from reaching the British armies. The Doctor, assuming Napoleon’s persona, managed to relay vital orders to the Prussian commander and averted disaster.

Even as the Doctor returned to Gallifrey to expose a CIA mole using the time scoop to aid the Countess’s schemes, his next challenge waited in the research of Kartz and Reimer into time travel.

text: Sixteen-year-old Miranda worries about staying sensible in a household full of dreamers. Her younger sister, Cassandra, just nine years and eleven months old, is anything but ordinary—she clings to the belief in magic and the wonders of myths. Miranda knows it’s easier to be the sensible one when her father, Professor Aisling, lectures about legends at university. Aisling is passionate about the mysterious, convinced that there’s truth to the creatures and stories hidden in the old tales. Yet at his institution, some professors, especially Mr. Bilgewallow, mock these ideas, insisting that magic can’t be studied or proven—only ridiculed. One night, Miranda, her sisters, and Aisling take a walk by the river when, to their wonder, a tiny ship appears. Dwarfs and gremlins, working the sails, greet Professor Aisling as the ship's Captain Malachi declares it belonged to him all along—a vessel conjured from his very wishes, ready to ride the "tides of inspiration." Aisling is both shocked and overjoyed. Cassandra races aboard, swept up in the adventure, while Miranda hesitates, needing to be convinced. On this enchanted boat, they meet legendary beings: the mischievous Harpies who take over the kitchen, the dangerous Manticore, the riddlesolving Sphinx, the Minotaur, and even a dryad entwined with a tree. Trouble arises when Aisling becomes obsessed with collecting concrete evidence of the magical world for his skeptics like Mr. Bilgewallow, and brings aboard Medusa, whose presence proves perilous. When a crew member is threatened, it’s Cassandra’s faith and even Medusa’s own unpredictable nature that help Aisling see things as they should be again. In the end, the family must join forces against a band of evil trolls who threaten their journey home, reaffirming that belief and reason must work together to survive the unknown.

text:
Miranda, sixteen and practical to the bone, worries about making sensible choices, especially now that her father, Professor Aisling, teaches mythology at the university and still clings to the belief in magical things. In their family, Aisling is in the minority—most of the household doubts the value of fairy tales and legends, seeing them as stories without substance. But Mr. Bilgewallow, a colleague who’s particularly scornful, enjoys maddening Aisling, dismissing the professor’s dreams of magical journeys.

One evening, as the family walks by the river, a strange little ship appears, crewed by dwarfs and gremlins. One dwarf, Malachi, claims it’s Professor Aisling’s own ship, conjured from his longing to reach the lands of legend. Overcome with surprise and joy, Aisling invites his daughters aboard. Miranda hesitates, resistant to the idea, while Cassandra, only nine but enchanted by the unknown, leaps in. On board, the ship sets sail on “tides of inspiration,” and soon their crew encounters creatures from stories: harpies who take over the galley, a manticore, the sphinx, the minotaur, and even a dryad with a living tree.

Trouble brews when Aisling, eager for scientific proof of the magical, focuses too much on bringing back something measurable—especially the dangerous Medusa. Her presence causes chaos among the crew. However, with help from his daughters and even Medusa herself, Aisling regains his perspective. Together, the group must stand united against an attack from evil trolls, reaffirming the value of imagination and myth—proving, in the end, that reason and wonder can coexist.

text: Phileas Fogg is a mysterious British gentleman who lives with his valet Passepartout at No. 7 Saville-Row in Burlington Gardens during the latter half of the 19th century. Unbeknownst to his peers, he is also the immortal foster child of a race of humanoid aliens known as the Eridani. A man of great intellect and affluence, Fogg enters into a wager with a fellow Eridanian citing that he can circumnavigate the globe in exactly eighty days. Although witnesses feel that his claim is little more than the boasting of a rich eccentric, Fogg is in fact undertaking a secret mission on behalf of his Eridanian colleagues. Along with Passepartout, Fogg begins a quest to find a piece of stolen alien technology – a teleportation device that had recently fallen into the hands of the Eridani's rivals, an alien race known as the Capellas. His journey brings him face to face with the infamous sea scourge Captain Nemo, a Capellan agent who is also known in British circles by his nom de guerre – James Moriarty. The two combatants match wits with one another at several key locations, including the mysterious ghost ship known as the Mary Celeste. The journey climaxes with a final battle at Fogg's home in London, mere moments before meeting the deadline required to win his world-spanning wager.

text: In a tiny Texas jail, down in a cramped cell, two people cross paths. Photo-Finish is a failing gambler, recently jailed after a disputed encounter leaves him in trouble back in a dusty, judgmental town. He’s kept company by Emily, a dissatisfied cook whose sadness is as deep as the cells around her. The moment they see one another, an immediate spark of connection ignites between them. Before long, Photo-Finish and Emily form a bond, dreaming of escaping together to San Francisco. Their hopes, however, are shattered when the men hunting Photo-Finish discover him and, in a moment of violence, take his life.

text: In a serene hothouse, a lone dandelion seed from the outside world managed to sneak in and take root. This invader and its progeny began to thrive, consuming the hothouse's precious water, nutrients, and sunlight. The resident flowers, though suffering, stayed quiet, not wanting to seem prejudiced. The hothouse's owner, akin to a god overseeing their domain, noticed the issue and removed the dandelions. When more seeds tried to invade, the native flowers fought back, using their roots and stems to bury the intruders where they couldn't grow. This defense worked, and the external dandelions ceased their attempts to invade.
